We’re hiring: Sales Associate. Remote, India-based, full-time contract.
The students who message us are carrying a lot: an education loan, a family counting on them, and a job search that hasn’t worked yet. Many have been burned by services that promised too much. They don’t need a pushy salesperson. They need someone who listens, tells them the truth, and helps them pick the right plan.
At Jaithraya, we help international students find the right job, the right résumé, and we apply for them. As our Sales Associate, you’re the first real person they talk to.
What you’ll do:
→ Reply to students who reach out on Instagram and WhatsApp. Inbound only, no cold calling
→ Understand each student’s situation before suggesting anything
→ Guide them to the plan that fits, and help them get started
→ Check in with your customers in their first weeks so they get real value
→ Ask happy customers to refer their friends
→ Keep every conversation logged in our lead tracker
Our rules, and the reason students trust us:
→ Never promise a job, an interview or a visa outcome
→ Never give visa or immigration advice. Those questions go to the student’s DSO (their school’s international student office) or an immigration attorney
→ Never handle a customer’s card, bank details or passwords
→ Never invent a testimonial, a number or a result
→ No mass messaging, ever
You’re a fit if you:
→ Listen first, then guide. You never push
→ Speak and write clear English (Telugu or Hindi is a plus)
→ Know WhatsApp, Instagram, AI chat tools (like ChatGPT or Claude) and online tools
→ Stay calm and honest when someone says “is this a scam?” or “it’s too expensive”
→ Care whether the customer is still happy three months later, not just whether they paid
Good to have: experience in sales, counselling, customer success or study-abroad services.
The details:
• Work from home: you need your own laptop, stable internet and headphones
• Pay discussed after the interview
• You work directly with the founder
How to apply: email HR at bhavishya@jaithraya.com or the founder at anwarrashidshaik@jaithraya.com with the subject “Sales – where you saw this post” (e.g. “Sales – LinkedIn”) and include:
Your CV
A few lines on why this role suits you
One time you helped someone make a decision without pushing them
Selection: application review → short intro call → a role-play (a typical student question, handled live) → final interview.

Most careers are run like a support queue.

The best accounts are run nine months ahead.

At Capgemini, one of my global accounts had its renewal due at the end of the year.

By the end of the first quarter, we already knew we would keep it.

Not because anything was signed.

Because of three things we did early: the client's KPIs went on page one of every review, bad news reached their sponsor within 24 hours with a recovery plan attached, and every slip had one name on it.

By the time procurement opened the file, there was nothing left to argue about.

The year closed at ₹20 Cr+ against a ₹16 Cr target.

Here is where I think careers are heading.

Hiring is turning into renewal.

Annual performance cuts, contract roles and AI-driven reviews mean more of us get re-signed every year instead of hired once.

So the rules of a key account now apply to a career.

Your sponsor is a person, not a company.

Your renewal is decided nine months before the review.

Silence from the top is not safety.

The counter-view is fair: loyalty still exists at good companies, and treating every year as a renewal sounds exhausting.

But the people I saw kept through every downturn were the ones who ran their own numbers before anyone asked for them.

One question to put on your desk on Monday: if my manager had to re-sign me today, what would be on page one?

I write about this every week in The Career Operating System. Subscribe link in the comments.

Is a career run like a renewal smarter, or just a kinder word for permanent insecurity?

If you lead a team or run a large account, connect with me. I want to hear how you would answer that.

Opening a GCC in India is the easy part.

The hard part is month 6 to month 18, when the ribbon-cutting photos are done and HQ starts asking what the centre is actually delivering.

Patterns I keep seeing in new centres:

1. Mandate drift. The centre launched for "technology and analytics" and ends up absorbing whatever HQ hands over. Write the 3-year charter early.

2. Hiring the team before the leaders. 300 engineers without strong product and domain leads becomes an expensive back office.

3. Vendor overlap. The old outsourcing contracts don't shrink as fast as the centre grows, so costs double before they fall.

4. Setup choices that don't scale. Entity structure, SEZ/STPI decisions and transfer pricing made for 50 people get painful at 1,500.

5. No AI plan. The centres getting real attention from global boards are the ones building AI and automation into the operating model, not bolting it on later.

If you lead a GCC that opened in the last year or two: which of these is hitting you hardest?

🚀 OPEN TO SENIOR .NET FULL STACK / .NET AI CONTRACT OPPORTUNITIES

🚨 Your .NET API successfully saves an order to SQL Server.
But the event notification fails.
Now what?

This is one of the most important reliability challenges in event-driven enterprise applications.
Consider an ASP.NET Core order-processing service:
1️⃣ The API receives an order.
2️⃣ Entity Framework Core saves the transaction.
3️⃣ The service publishes an event to Azure Service Bus.
4️⃣ Another microservice processes the event.

Everything works until step 3 fails.
The database transaction is committed.
But the downstream service never receives the event.
Now your enterprise systems have inconsistent information.
This is why simply combining database transactions with message publishing isn't enough.

A common solution is the Transactional Outbox Pattern.
✅ Save business data and an outbox event in the same database transaction
✅ Commit both changes atomically
✅ Use a background worker to publish pending events
✅ Retry failed publications safely
✅ Make consumers idempotent
✅ Track event status and processing attempts
✅ Monitor undelivered events and processing delays
✅ Handle duplicate delivery without repeating business operations

In .NET, this can be implemented using ASP.NET Core, EF Core, SQL Server, BackgroundService, and Azure Service Bus or RabbitMQ.

The key idea:
The database update and event record succeed together.
Publishing happens independently and can be retried.
It doesn't guarantee exactly-once event delivery, but it helps prevent events from being lost between database commits and message publication.

How do you usually maintain data consistency across microservices?
A) Transactional Outbox Pattern
B) Saga Pattern
C) Distributed Transactions
D) Eventual Consistency with Idempotent Consumers

A question for SaaS founders. Ten seconds, and the answer is usually uncomfortable.




𝗜𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝗵𝗮𝗹𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁 𝘁𝘄𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗮𝘀 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 — 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲?

For most per-seat businesses, revenue falls. And cost rises, because usage went up.

That is the whole problem in one sentence.

Per-seat pricing was never really a pricing model. It was a bet — that your customer would keep hiring, and that more people meant more value delivered.

For twenty years that bet was good. AI breaks it from both ends at once.

𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱𝘀 𝗳𝗲𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 to do the same work. Every seat they remove is revenue you lose, even when the work you support has gone up.

𝗔𝗻𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲, not seats. So the heaviest users — the ones getting the most value, the ones you most want to keep — are the ones compressing your margin.

Revenue indexed to headcount. Cost indexed to consumption. Those two moving in opposite directions is not something you can discount your way out of.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵

𝘊𝘰𝘯𝘴𝘶𝘮𝘱𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘱𝘳𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘯𝘨 — aligns cost and revenue, makes the bill unpredictable. Unpredictable bills make buyers ration usage, which is the opposite of what you want.

𝘖𝘶𝘵𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘯𝘨 — the most honest answer and the hardest to operate. You need an outcome both sides can measure, attribute to you, and agree before the work starts. Few products clear that bar.

𝘏𝘺𝘣𝘳𝘪𝘥, 𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘮 𝘧𝘦𝘦 𝘱𝘭𝘶𝘴 𝘶𝘴𝘢𝘨𝘦 — where most will land. It only works if the platform fee covers fixed cost and the usage component covers marginal cost. Most teams set both by feel.

𝗠𝘆 𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄

Nobody has solved this yet. The ones who look like they have are mostly early enough that the headcount effect has not reached them.

And the ones in trouble will not find out from a dashboard. They will find out at renewal, when a customer who loves the product asks for forty fewer seats.

Three questions, and I would rather read the answers than be agreed with.

𝗛𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘀𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗳𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗮𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗹 𝘆𝗲𝘁 — or is this still theoretical in your numbers?

𝗜𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗳𝗳 𝗽𝗲𝗿-𝘀𝗲𝗮𝘁, 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝗸𝗲?

𝗔𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗱, 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘆𝗼𝘂? I suspect it is rarely conviction. It is that re-papering every contract is brutal.

—

Working through this with a small group of founders on 30 October. What you charge per, what it costs you, and what happens when those two stop moving together. Details in the comments.

🤖 AI Agents can act autonomously. But should they make every decision on their own?

As AI Agents become more capable of taking actions across business systems, autonomy needs to be matched with the right level of control.

A practical approach is to distinguish between:

🔹 Low-risk tasks → AI can execute automatically
🔹 High-impact decisions → Human approval is required
🔹 Irreversible actions → Add a confirmation checkpoint
🔹 Unclear processes → Escalate to human review

This is especially important for areas such as financial decisions, legal and contract decisions, hiring and employee evaluation, and actions with significant consequences.

The goal is not to limit AI Agents unnecessarily.

It is to give AI the right level of autonomy while keeping humans in control of important decisions.

What #GovTech is doing right now is the exact reverse of the 1990s National Computer Board (NCB) to NCS evolution.

When you look at this through the lens of Singapore's IT history, the logic clicks into place:

The Historical Loop: NCB → NCS → GovTech

1. The NCB Era (1981–1997): The National Computer Board was set up to computerise the civil service. It built a massive, centralized pool of government IT professionals who actually built and ran the systems.

2. The NCS Pivot (1997): The government decided that the state shouldn't be an IT shop. They spun off NCB’s engineering arm into a commercial entity called NCS (National Computer Systems) and privatised it (eventually bought by Singtel).

3. The Outsourcing Era (Late 90s–2010s): For nearly two decades, the civil service relied entirely on outsourcing. GovTech's predecessors became contract managers. They wrote specifications on paper, paid NCS, IBM, or Accenture to build them, and hired hundreds of Project Managers (PMs) to watch the vendors.

When will this pendulum stop swinging?

Why the Equilibrium Constantly Shifts (The 3 Forces):

1. The Technology Cycle: Innovation vs. Standardization
• Swing In-House (Exploration): When technology is new, complex, or strategic (like early internet in the NCB era, or advanced cloud architecture/cybersecurity today), no external vendor can do it well or securely enough. The organization must build it in-house to innovate and control it.
• Swing Out (Commoditization): Over 10 to 15 years, that technology becomes standard, boring, and commoditized. It becomes cheaper to buy it off-the-shelf from commercial vendors (like basic IT support, HR systems, or payroll) than to pay expensive internal engineers to maintain it.

2. The Economic Cycle: Growth vs. Cost-Cutting
• In-House: During periods of growth or crisis, the priority is speed and capability. Organizations hire aggressively to build internal teams so they can pivot instantly.
• Outsource: When budgets tighten or inflation hits, finance teams look at the massive internal payroll fixed costs. They realize they can convert those fixed costs into variable costs by outsourcing to external vendors, whom they can easily fire or downsize via contract terms.

3. The Management Cycle: Control vs. Agility 
• In-House gives you absolute control over security and quality, but it creates a massive, slow bureaucracy (too many layers, slow hiring).
• Outsourcing gives you agility and flexibility to scale up or down quickly, but you lose control, domain knowledge, and data security.

The place of equilibrium is "Rightsourcing" - the fine balance: 
Having an agile workforce, always ready to retrain, and management commitment to do so.

One Oklahoma City job post I read this week asks for three different people and calls them one Senior Data Engineer.

The posting, for an energy company, wants someone to keep legacy SQL Server and Informatica pipelines running, migrate those same workflows to Snowflake and dbt Cloud, build Streamlit apps and AI features inside Snowflake, and run enterprise scheduling. Five plus years of experience. Oil and gas background preferred.

None of that is unreasonable on its own. Together, it describes a platform maintainer, a modernization engineer, and an analytics app builder. When a role is written that wide, the search usually goes the same way: strong candidates rule themselves out, the few who apply fit only part of the job, and months pass while the posting waits for a person who does not exist in one body.

The fix is unglamorous. Decide which outcome the business needs first, write the role around that outcome, and cover the rest honestly, with contract help or a later hire. A narrow role fills. A bundled role lingers.

Is your hardest data role truly one job, or two jobs sharing a title? Yes or no: would splitting it get the first hire in sooner?

One Oklahoma City job post I read this week asks for three different people and calls them one Senior Data Engineer.

The posting, for an energy company, wants someone to keep legacy SQL Server and Informatica pipelines running, migrate those same workflows to Snowflake and dbt Cloud, build Streamlit apps and AI features inside Snowflake, and run enterprise scheduling. Five plus years of experience. Oil and gas background preferred.

None of that is unreasonable on its own. Together, it describes a platform maintainer, a modernization engineer, and an analytics app builder. When a role is written that wide, the search usually goes the same way: strong candidates rule themselves out, the few who apply fit only part of the job, and months pass while the posting waits for a person who does not exist in one body.

The fix is unglamorous. Decide which outcome the business needs first, write the role around that outcome, and cover the rest honestly, with contract help or a later hire. A narrow role fills. A bundled role lingers.

Is your hardest data role truly one job, or two jobs sharing a title? Yes or no: would splitting it get the first hire in sooner?

Are you an IT professional looking for your next opportunity in Canada?

Whether you are an experienced software developer, a newcomer to Canada, an internationally trained IT professional, or a recent graduate, your job search needs more than sending hundreds of applications.

10 practical strategies I recommend: 

* Focus on the right opportunities

Explore roles that align with your experience, including Software Developer, Data Analyst, Cybersecurity Analyst, Cloud Engineer, QA Tester, Business Analyst and IT Support.

* Research before applying

Understand the company's business, technology stack, required skills and expectations before submitting your application.

* Make your resume ATS-friendly

Use a clear Canadian-style resume, relevant technical keywords and measurable achievements. Tailor it to each position instead of sending the same resume everywhere.

* Strengthen your LinkedIn profile

Update your headline, About section, skills and experience. Make it easy for recruiters to understand your expertise and the value you bring.

* Network with purpose

Connect with IT recruiters, hiring managers, former colleagues and professionals in your target industry. Build genuine relationships instead of reaching out only when you need a job.

* Showcase your practical skills

Keep your GitHub, portfolio, technical projects or case studies updated. Demonstrate what you can do, not just what you know.

* Prepare for technical and behavioural interviews

Practise coding challenges or role specific assessments where relevant. Prepare examples of problem solving, teamwork, communication and handling challenges using the STAR method.

* Stay open to contract opportunities

Consider suitable contract, temporary and permanent roles. Evaluate the responsibilities, compensation, benefits and career growth before accepting an offer.

* Use strategy 

Review newly posted positions regularly, follow target employers and prepare for opportunities with active hiring timelines.

* Track your job search

Maintain a simple spreadsheet with company names, job titles, application dates, recruiter contacts, follow-ups and interview status. Review your progress every week and adjust your strategy.

The IT market is competitive, and opportunities vary by occupation, location and experience. Current hiring research points to opportunities in areas such as cybersecurity, AI, cloud, data analytics and software development, but no particular skill guarantees a job.

My advice as a Career Coach and HR Consultant is simple:

Apply strategically. 
Build relevant skills. 
Network consistently. 
Prepare confidently. 
Follow up professionally.

Your next opportunity may not come from sending more applications. It may come from making the right application with the right preparation.

For a small AI medical device company, continuous monitoring is not just another compliance step. It turns a research-led organization into an operations and clinical-operations one.
On October 6, the UK's MHRA announced it had adopted all 44 recommendations from its review of AI in healthcare. MedTech Dive (Elise Reuter, October 7) reports that the regulator is backing oversight across the whole product lifecycle, not a single check before launch. The quote that stuck with me: "one-off pre-market assessments will not be enough." Draft guidance on managing changes is due by December 2026, with consultation in early 2027 and a roadmap in spring 2027. The AI Airlock pilot makes its first selections in November. MHRA CEO Lawrence Tallon is quoted in the piece.
The article does not say what this means for manufacturers' obligations or costs. What follows is my own judgment, not something the regulator has said.
If a product must be watched after launch, the company needs people and processes that watch it: monitoring performance in real settings, tracking whether the model drifts, collecting clinical feedback, and re-auditing when something changes. For a team built around building the algorithm, that is a different kind of work, with different hiring, different budgets and a different rhythm. Three moves I would consider.
One, move away from perpetual licenses toward software-as-a-service or subscription pricing with a maintenance fee. If you owe ongoing monitoring, a one-time sale leaves you funding it from nothing.
Two, rewrite your hospital service-level agreements. Spell out log-sharing obligations, who is responsible when the model drifts, and the maintenance windows. Vague wording here becomes a dispute later.
Three, put post-market monitoring and clinical follow-up into fixed operating expense, with re-audit scheduled as a line item, not a surprise. A company that budgets for it can plan; a company that treats it as an exception will keep being surprised.
None of this is required by the announcement itself. The guidance is still being drafted, and the details may land differently. But the direction is clear enough to plan around, and the lead time is useful: the first draft guidance arrives in about two months.
My prediction: small AI device companies that redesign pricing and contracts around continuous monitoring early will find the new rules easier to absorb than those who wait for final text. Those who keep a one-time-sale model may find the financial gap shows up first.
If your product had to be monitored for as long as a hospital uses it, would your current contract and pricing still cover it?

Google Wants Uninterruptible Power, And Will Pay You to Interrupt Yours      

Matching fast-growing data center power demand against slow-growing supply is becoming increasingly challenging, especially in the power-strapped PJM RTO,  the largest power grid and electricity market in the US.

Rather than wait for grid capacity to grow sufficiently to serve them on a firm basis, data center developers have offered to bring their own power, pay for grid improvements, agree to take interruptible power, and employ software solutions to prioritize different tasks and shift compute load between locations. 

But what they really want is uninterruptible power, in large quantities, ASAP.  

And that may require, among other solutions, hiring demand response providers to create virtual power plants (VPPs) which deliver that power by incenting other users to use  batteries or reduce their loads. 

The demand response industry predates AI data centers, as the need to deal with peak loads in excess of grid capacity is not new - think rolling blackouts during summer peaks. 

In PJM, Google has partnered with Voltus, an industry leader managing over 9 gigawatts of demand response and VPP capacity, to make available  an initial 100 MW of capacity, expected to grow to 1 GW.

Voltus would provide customer-sited batteries and/or pay a network of residential  and business power customers to shed load by turning down air conditioners, time shifting water heaters, etc., to free up power for Google data centers. 

Unlike traditional demand response contracts with 3-year terms, however, Voltus is securing commitments through 2040, providing a long-term revenue stream to the residential and business counterparties, and a long-term planning horizon for Google to present to utility regulators.

“AI may remove enough customer effort to create more demand, not less.”

That line from CX Today caused me to think quite hard about the future. It raised more questions than answers because it’s a glimpse into a future that’s slowly revealing itself.

As an operations professional, I encourage contact centers to start working on this now, not after personal AI assistants have scaled. Waiting is too costly. If you find yourself cornered and hiring at scale, it takes time and it’s expensive. In the meantime, service levels slip and churn grows.

Here are the questions I’d immediately lean into for my contact center:

What’s our strategy for serving customers, and the AI agents acting on their behalf?

How will we forecast and staff for demand we’ve never seen before?

What mix of human and AI workforce will we use, and how will we prepare people for harder, more judgment-heavy work?

How will we verify identity, intent, and permission when an AI agent contacts us?

How will we govern AI and protect our customers’ data?

How will we structure our tech stack and vendor contracts to stay flexible?

I love problem solving. Believe it or not, I spring out of bed in the morning when I know a significant challenge is waiting to be tackled.

Which of these questions is your organization furthest along on? Which one keeps you up at night?

A Little Honesty, Please

The current job market is non-existent. The unemployment rate, job openings, labor participation, and other metrics are meaningless. The reality on the ground is hiring is frozen.

Recruiters have responded as they always do by telling applicants all the things they need to do or are doing wrong. They are positive and encouraging, and I appreciate that, but the advice isn’t entirely honest. 

There’s advice about authenticity in the era of AI enhanced resumes and cover letters, and in the end, they land on “lean into your network.” 

Knowing someone has always been the ticket, but as a blue-collar kid who was the first in his family to attend college the dirty secret is most networks result from social capital that was inherited, not earned or cultivated. 

Why is hiring frozen? The two-letter answer to all questions, AI. 

This isn’t about the unstoppable job killing juggernaut of AI. 

No, this is about its total failure to replace people. Let’s be honest, its intent was getting rid of people entirely; that has failed.

AI isn’t getting better, it’s being asked to do less as the goal posts move from person replacement to utility. 

AI is also failing at that task because it takes productive creative human labor and turns it into perpetual editing; mistakes that come at unsustainable prices.

C-suites through a combination of rage at demographics that shrunk the labor pool and increased wages, and FOMO driving quarterly earnings calls and stock prices, caused them to make absurd promises based on technology they didn’t vet and don’t understand. 

The hiring freezes we’re experiencing are a C-suite tantrum because their AI plans to replace labor have failed. 

The AI contracts they’ve signed are destroying budgets and margins. Their boards and Wall Street have questions. Meanwhile, productivity has suffered, there’s work to be done and money to make. They need people, not AI.

So instead of accepting reality, we get ghosts jobs, recruiters inquiring about your rate to gauge the market for jobs that don’t exist, stories about hundreds of applicants for a single position, companies lamenting they can’t find people with the requisite skills, etc. 

None of this is true.

Ghost jobs are intended to signal growth to Wall Street and measure the talent pool. 

Transferable skills are not a new concept so finding qualified people is not a problem. 

Jobs have hundreds of applicants because the job listing has been posted and reposted multiple times while hiring is frozen. 

Don’t believe those who only have advice that places blame entirely on job seekers. 

You aren’t responsible for AI hype and lies, C-suite euphoria about AI freeing it from labor market reality, a lack of skills, your age, or anything else that doesn’t land where this began.

The hiring question is what happens to the work afterwards.

NAB says frontline bankers are not affected. The cuts sit in middle management, marketing and administration.

In my experience, that is where the risk tends to show up, in the operating model six months later.

The work does not disappear with the role. It gets absorbed, automated, outsourced or quietly returns as contract hiring.

Sometimes that is good discipline.

Sometimes it is cost moved from one line to another.

If the work was unnecessary, fine. If it was not, productivity becomes a slogan.

You have not simplified the bank.

You have made fewer people responsible for the same mess.
